precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.prompt: A client is in a moderate calorie deficit and still lifting three days a week. What is protein’s most useful coaching job here?

options.a: Serve as the main fuel for those high-intensity lifting sessions
options.b: Raise metabolism enough that the deficit is no longer needed
options.c: Supply essential fatty acids the body uses to make hormones
options.d: Support fullness and muscle retention while calories stay lower

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: In a deficit, protein’s practical job is satiety plus helping retain lean mass when training continues. It is not the primary high-intensity fuel, and its extra thermic cost is too small to replace an energy gap. Essential fatty acids come from dietary fat, not protein.

distractorExplanations.a: Carbohydrate (muscle glycogen) is the main fuel for hard lifting; protein’s coaching role is fullness and muscle retention.
distractorExplanations.b: Protein’s higher thermic effect is real but small; it cannot cancel a calorie deficit or replace fat-loss math.
distractorExplanations.c: Essential fatty acids come from fat; protein does not supply them and is not a hormone-fat substitute.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.prompt: A client lost about 8 lb across 10 weeks on a mixed-macro plan. What best explains the fat-loss portion of that change?

options.a: A sustained calorie deficit across those weeks
options.b: Mostly the first-week glycogen and water drop
options.c: Fat loss that only happens when carbs stay very low
options.d: Day-to-day scale noise from sodium and gut contents

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Meaningful fat loss still requires a sustained energy deficit, whatever the carb level. First-week drops and daily swings are mostly water, glycogen, sodium, and gut contents. Low-carb can help some people eat less, but it is not the only path to a deficit.

distractorExplanations.b: Early scale drops are mostly glycogen and water; they do not explain weeks of fat loss on a mixed-macro plan.
distractorExplanations.c: Fat loss follows energy balance on high- or low-carb patterns; low-carb is one way to create a deficit, not a requirement.
distractorExplanations.d: Daily weight noise is water, sodium, and gut contents; it is not the fat-loss trend across 10 weeks.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.prompt: A client wants to strip almost all dietary fat “to get lean faster.” What should you teach about fat at Precision Nutrition Level 1?

options.a: It is mainly needed to absorb water-soluble vitamins such as C and B12
options.b: It supports hormones, fat-soluble vitamins, and meal satisfaction
options.c: It is the main structural building block used to grow new muscle
options.d: It is the primary fuel for short, high-intensity sprint efforts

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Dietary fat is not optional window dressing. Clients need some fat for hormones, absorption of vitamins A, D, E, and K, and meals they can stick with. Extreme fat cuts often backfire as hunger and adherence problems, and they do not magically outrun energy balance.

distractorExplanations.a: Fat helps absorb fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), not water-soluble vitamin C and B vitamins.
distractorExplanations.c: Protein, not fat, is the main structural macronutrient for muscle tissue.
distractorExplanations.d: Short, hard efforts run mainly on carbohydrate; fat is a larger fuel at lower intensities.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.prompt: A recreational lifter asks if they should drop carbs to near zero to get lean. What is the best coach-level answer?

options.a: Carbs are nonessential, so cutting them is the fastest fat-loss path
options.b: Carbs drive fat gain mainly through insulin, even in a deficit
options.c: Carbs are useful training fuel and can still fit a fat-loss plan
options.d: Carbs should be eaten mostly at breakfast and avoided after 6 p.m.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Precision Nutrition Level 1 does not treat carbohydrate as a toxin. Carbs fuel higher-intensity training and can sit inside a calorie deficit. Fat loss is not reserved for keto, insulin is not the main fat-gain switch, and clock-based carb bans rarely beat total intake and training needs.

distractorExplanations.a: A deficit—not a carb ban—drives fat loss; many clients lose fat while still eating carbs around training.
distractorExplanations.b: The carbohydrate-insulin story is not the main cause of fat gain; sustained energy surplus is.
distractorExplanations.d: Time-of-day carb rules matter far less than total intake and putting carbs where training needs them.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.prompt: A client feels hungry between meals and constipated on a low-produce diet. What is fiber’s main coaching benefit?

options.a: Driving muscle protein synthesis after lifting sessions
options.b: Improving uptake of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K
options.c: Speeding glycogen refill in the hours after hard training
options.d: Supporting fullness and more regular digestion day to day

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Fiber from plants is a satiety and GI-regularity tool. It is not a substitute for protein after lifting, not a fat-soluble vitamin carrier, and not a fast glycogen refill. For a hungry, constipated client, more produce and other fiber sources is the practical first move.

distractorExplanations.a: Muscle protein synthesis depends on protein and training stimulus, not on fiber grams.
distractorExplanations.b: Fat-soluble vitamin absorption needs dietary fat; fiber is not the uptake vehicle.
distractorExplanations.c: Rapid glycogen refill uses faster-digesting carbohydrate; fiber slows, not speeds, that process.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.prompt: A client bloated after dairy and announces a “milk allergy.” What is the safest Precision Nutrition Level 1 stance?

options.a: It may be intolerance, a habit, or medical—do not diagnose it
options.b: Removing dairy for one week is enough to confirm a true allergy
options.c: Bloating proves a gluten allergy that the coach can officially rule in
options.d: An at-home IgG food panel is the right way to verify the allergy

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Self-labeled “allergy” after bloating is often intolerance, portion size, eating speed, or something medical. Coaches stay in scope: they do not confirm IgE allergy, celiac disease, or IgG “sensitivities.” Suspected true allergy or unexplained GI symptoms belong with a licensed clinician.

distractorExplanations.b: A short self-elimination cannot confirm IgE allergy; that needs medical history and appropriate testing.
distractorExplanations.c: Dairy bloating is not a gluten-allergy diagnosis, and coaches cannot diagnose celiac disease or allergy.
distractorExplanations.d: IgG food panels are not a valid allergy test; selling or trusting them overreaches coaching scope.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.prompt: A client “forgets” weekend drinks in the food log and fat loss has stalled. What should you teach about alcohol?

options.a: Count it as carbohydrate grams, the same as table sugar
options.b: It is energy-dense and often a trigger for looser eating
options.c: A drink or two after training helps muscle repair overnight
options.d: Mixed with diet soda, the alcohol itself supplies no calories

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Alcohol is its own energy source (about 7 kcal/g) and often pairs with extra food, worse sleep, and skipped protein. If it is not logged, the deficit on paper is fiction. Mixers do not erase ethanol calories, and drinks after training do not help recovery.

distractorExplanations.a: Ethanol is not carbohydrate counted as sugar; it is a separate, energy-dense source of about 7 kcal/g.
distractorExplanations.c: Alcohol impairs muscle protein synthesis and sleep quality, so it hinders recovery rather than helping it.
distractorExplanations.d: Diet mixers add little energy; the alcohol still contributes about 7 kcal per gram.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.prompt: A client wants one hydration rule they can follow on busy workdays. What is the safest basic advice?

options.a: Drink one gallon of water every day, no matter body size or climate
options.b: Wait until thirst is intense before taking any fluids at all
options.c: Take fluids regularly and use pale-yellow urine as a rough check
options.d: Aim for crystal-clear urine all day as proof they are hydrated

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Basic coaching hydration is regular fluids plus a crude check: pale yellow urine, thirst, and how the client feels in heat or training. A fixed gallon, waiting for desperate thirst, or chasing clear urine all day are one-size myths and can push overdrinking.

distractorExplanations.a: Fluid needs vary with body size, climate, and activity; a universal gallon rule is a myth.
distractorExplanations.b: Strong thirst often lags, especially around exercise; waiting that long is a poor default.
distractorExplanations.d: Always-clear urine can mean overdrinking; pale yellow is the usual crude target, not colorless.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.prompt: A client wants to “cover nutrition” with a large pill stack instead of changing meals. What is the best first-line micronutrient advice?

options.a: Start a one-a-day multivitamin and skip any food changes
options.b: Rely on fortified breakfast cereal as the entire micronutrient plan
options.c: Take large single-nutrient megadoses “just in case” they are low
options.d: Build a varied plate first; pills only fill a specific, identified gap

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Food-first variety covers most micronutrient needs plus fiber and food matrix benefits pills miss. A multivitamin or a targeted supplement can fill a known gap, but a random stack, cereal-only “fortification,” or megadoses are not the Level 1 default—and selling pills is not the coach’s job.

distractorExplanations.a: A multi can fill some gaps, but it is a backup, not a reason to skip vegetables, protein, and variety.
distractorExplanations.b: Fortified cereal adds a few nutrients and still misses produce, fiber, and broader food quality.
distractorExplanations.c: High-dose single vitamins risk imbalance or toxicity and do not replace a varied diet.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.prompt: A client is upset about a 4 lb jump on the scale the morning after a salty restaurant dinner. What usually explains that change?

options.a: Glycogen, sodium, and gut contents shifting overnight
options.b: About four pounds of new body fat from that one meal
options.c: Several pounds of muscle broken down while they slept
options.d: Immediate metabolic collapse from one higher-calorie day

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Overnight swings of a few pounds are almost always water, glycogen, sodium, and gut contents. Four pounds of fat would require on the order of 14,000 extra kcal. Muscle does not vanish overnight, and metabolic adaptation is slow and small—not a one-night 4 lb event.

distractorExplanations.b: Four pounds of fat would need roughly 14,000 extra kcal; one restaurant meal cannot do that.
distractorExplanations.c: Muscle cannot be lost in that amount overnight; rapid jumps are fluid and GI contents.
distractorExplanations.d: Adaptive thermogenesis is gradual; it does not drop body weight 4 lb by the next morning.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.prompt: A client treats a 1,200-kcal app target as “my metabolism” and wants to eat that forever. How should you explain resting metabolic rate?

options.a: It is the same number as total daily energy expenditure
options.b: It is energy used at rest to keep the body running
options.c: It is only the calories burned during planned workouts
options.d: It is only the energy spent digesting and absorbing meals

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: RMR is resting energy cost—keeping organs and tissues going—not the whole day’s burn. TDEE also includes daily movement, exercise, and the thermic effect of food. App outputs are estimates, not a medical prescription to live at 1,200 kcal.

distractorExplanations.a: TDEE is rest plus movement, exercise, and food processing; RMR is only the resting piece.
distractorExplanations.c: Workout calories are exercise activity, one slice of TDEE, not resting metabolic rate.
distractorExplanations.d: Energy used to digest food is TEF, a small TDEE slice, not RMR.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.prompt: A client wants to “hack metabolism” by eating only protein shakes. What is true of the thermic effect of food at coach level?

options.a: A small slice of daily burn, and highest for dietary fat
options.b: The largest slice of daily burn, bigger than resting metabolism
options.c: A small slice of daily burn, and highest for protein
options.d: A large slice of daily burn, and highest for carbohydrate

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: TEF is real and modest—often around 10% of TDEE—and protein costs more to process than carb or fat. That does not make an all-shake diet a metabolism cheat code. Resting metabolism is still the biggest daily burn, and fat has the lowest thermic effect.

distractorExplanations.a: Fat has the lowest thermic effect (roughly 0–3%); protein, not fat, is the highest.
distractorExplanations.b: RMR is the largest TDEE component; TEF is a small slice, not larger than rest.
distractorExplanations.d: TEF is not a large share of TDEE, and carbohydrate is not the highest-thermic macro.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.prompt: A client on about 1,000 kcal is exhausted, cold, and sleeping poorly. What is the best next coaching move?

options.a: Add extra cardio to “boost energy” while keeping the same cut
options.b: Push caffeine so they can keep training through the fatigue
options.c: Call it normal adaptation and hold the same very low intake
options.d: Raise food intake and consider medical review if it persists

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Persistent exhaustion, feeling cold, and broken sleep on a very low-calorie diet are warning data, not proof the plan is “working.” Underfueling plus stress physiology is a reason to add food and, if symptoms continue, to loop in a clinician—not to add cardio or stimulants.

distractorExplanations.a: More cardio on an already tiny intake deepens the energy hole and usually worsens fatigue and sleep.
distractorExplanations.b: Caffeine can mask tiredness without fixing low energy availability; it is not the coaching fix.
distractorExplanations.c: Ongoing exhaustion and poor sleep are not “just adaptation” to push through on ~1,000 kcal.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.prompt: A client asks whether creatine monohydrate is “worth taking.” What is the Precision Nutrition Level 1-appropriate answer?

options.a: It is well studied, but you educate—you do not prescribe it
options.b: It is an anabolic steroid and banned in most competitive sport
options.c: It is proven to damage kidneys in otherwise healthy adults
options.d: It only helps long-distance endurance athletes, not lifters

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: Creatine monohydrate has a large evidence base for high-intensity and strength work, and it is not a steroid. A Level 1 coach can share that context and stay out of prescribing, dosing as a clinician, or selling it as a drug. Kidney disease and other medical flags are referral issues.

distractorExplanations.b: Creatine is a legal, non-hormonal compound, not an anabolic steroid, and it is not a typical WADA ban.
distractorExplanations.c: In healthy people, standard doses have not been shown to wreck kidneys; existing kidney disease needs a clinician.
distractorExplanations.d: Creatine’s best-supported uses are short, high-intensity and strength efforts, not endurance-only.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.prompt: A client hates logging grams. How should you describe the plate method so they do not mix it up with other tools?

options.a: A visual way to hit exact gram targets for each macronutrient
options.b: A visual split of protein, produce, and smart carbs or fats
options.c: A rule to finish everything on the plate before any seconds
options.d: The same tool as hand portions using palm, fist, and thumb

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-n.explanation: The plate method is a picture of the plate: protein, vegetables/fruit, and a remaining section for smart carbs and fats. It is not gram tracking, not a clean-plate rule, and not PN’s hand-portion system (palm, fist, cupped hand, thumb), which is a related but separate habit tool.

distractorExplanations.a: Exact grams are macro counting; the plate method uses visual food-group portions instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Finishing the plate is a clean-plate habit, not the visual split of protein, produce, and carbs/fats.
distractorExplanations.d: Palms, fists, and thumbs are the hand-portion method—a different Precision Nutrition tool from the plate split.
